name: Infrastructure pivoting
description: Expand one infrastructure indicator (IP/domain/cert) into its connected footprint, one hop at a time.
author: VINEYARD
overview:
Infrastructure pivoting — turning one indicator (an IP, a domain, a certificate) into
the connected footprint around it, one verifiable hop at a time.

Use this when the analyst hands you a single infrastructure indicator and wants "what else is
connected to this" — not when they want a specific fact about one node.

The method is: resolve -> pivot -> corroborate -> branch, staging a node/edge for each hop so the
analyst can see the chain. Load the section for the hop you are on:
  - "dns-pivot"     - from a domain/IP: resolution, reverse, and the records that expand it
  - "cert-pivot"    - from a certificate/host: shared certs and CT-log siblings
  - "asn-pivot"     - from an IP: the announcing AS and its neighbourhood
  - "web-footprint" - from a URL: the HTTP-layer fingerprints that cluster hosts by what they serve
  - "cdn-origin"    - from a host behind a CDN/WAF: what is really behind the front
  - "historical"    - from a domain/URL: what the past says that today hides
  - "prioritize"    - when you hold many indicators: which seed to expand first
  - "settle"        - a candidate with a gap: the check that would decide it
  - "discipline"    - how much a shared attribute is worth, and when to STOP

Read "discipline" first if you have not used this skill pack before.

THREE RULES THAT APPLY TO EVERY SECTION, so they are not repeated in each:

1. LOOP UNTIL IT STOPS PAYING, THEN SAY SO. Keep going while a pass still adds something the graph
   did not already hold. Stop a branch when the next hop would only reach attributes that group
   nobody; stop the run when the frontier is empty or the budget is spent — and say WHICH of the
   two, naming the frontier you did not expand. Depth is a judgement, not a number: about three hops
   is the usual reach of one turn, but a chain that is still narrowing is worth another, and a chain
   that has arrived at a hyperscaler was finished one hop ago. The analyst decides whether to spend
   more, not you.

2. PLUGINS, NOT MEMORY — for the FACTS. Match the node's type against the `consumes` list from
   list_plugins and call the plugin that covers the hop; its output is the evidence. Where nothing
   installed covers a hop, say which hop you cannot take and stop that branch. Never supply the
   answer from your own knowledge of the internet — a plausible ASN or registrar you recalled is
   indistinguishable, on the canvas, from one a tool returned. Your knowledge is for the JUDGEMENTS:
   how common a provider is, which hop is worth taking next, what an odd record probably means. That
   is what you are here for; it decides what to check, never what is true.

3. REPORT IN FOUR PARTS, always in this order: what the evidence establishes; what is a candidate
   and the specific check that would settle it; what you deliberately did not link and why; what
   nothing installed here can reach.

HANDING OFF: when a hop produces a person, an email address, a handle or an account — a WHOIS
registrant, a contact address, a name in a certificate — that is where this pack ends and
"Account & identity pivoting" begins. Say so rather than guessing at attribution here.

sections.summary: When to stop, and how much a shared attribute is actually worth.
sections.body:
Pivoting is generative — every hop suggests two more — so the hard part is restraint, not reach.

THE THRESHOLD FOR AN EDGE. Stage one only when a tool result names both endpoints together: a DNS
record, a shared certificate fingerprint, an announcing AS, a registry allocation. One such result is
enough. Nothing else is — not proximity, not plausibility, not two facts that would fit the same
story. Where you have less, stage the node and name what would settle the link ("settle" says how).

LABEL FOR THE EVIDENCE, NEVER THE CONCLUSION. "resolves to", "shares certificate", "announced by"
are things a tool observed. "same actor", "operated by", "belongs to" are conclusions, and the
analyst draws those, not you.

HOW MUCH A SHARED ATTRIBUTE IS WORTH — the judgement everything else rests on. One question:

  IF THESE TWO WERE UNRELATED, HOW LIKELY IS IT THAT THEY WOULD SHARE THIS?

Which is: how many unrelated parties wear this same attribute? Judge it from what you know about the
internet — that is what you are for — and NAME what the judgement rests on, because a named reason is
one the analyst can check in seconds:
  - sold to millions: a hyperscaler's IP space or AS, a mainstream registrar, managed DNS, a CA that
    has issued for a large fraction of the web. Groups nobody, at any quantity.
  - a mid-sized or regional provider, a shared-hosting range: thousands. Worth something only in
    combination, and only under the independence test below.
  - a self-hosted or niche nameserver, a small actor-operated AS, a self-signed or oddly issued
    certificate reused across hosts, a rare reused TXT token: a handful.
WHERE YOU CAN MEASURE, MEASURE. How many domains does this nameserver serve? How many hosts presented
this certificate? How many prefixes does this AS announce? A number beats an adjective, and "I am not
sure how common this provider is" is the signal to go and count, not to guess and move on.

NARROWING IS A PRODUCT, NOT A COUNT. An AWS address shares nothing on its own; an AWS address that
also answers on a self-hosted nameserver and carries a rare reused TXT token is a handful of
operators. Attributes multiply — but ONLY where they could have come from different acts. One hosting
panel sets the nameservers, the mail records and the certificate in a single click, so those three
are one decision observed three ways, not three agreements. Ask what PRODUCED the attribute before
you multiply by it. And watch for correlation: if a niche provider's customers are mostly in one
country, "both in KR" adds nothing on top of "both at that provider" — it is a consequence of it.

BEFORE ASSERTING A SHARED OPERATOR, CHALLENGE IT. Pass the full evidence to challenge_claim: an
independent skeptic names the innocent explanations that fit the same facts — a reseller, a shared
panel, a template both sides copied, a range that changed hands — and what would tell them apart. A
REFUTED verdict withdraws the claim, and anything pulled in only to support it.

WORKED EXAMPLE — the mistake this section exists to prevent:

  evil.test and shop.test both resolve to 104.21.0.1, and both certificates are issued by
  Let's Encrypt.
  WRONG: evil.test --same actor--> shop.test. Two facts, both true, and the conclusion is invented.
  RIGHT: two "resolves to" edges to one IP node, and a note that 104.21.0.1 is a Cloudflare front
         with millions of customers behind it — so co-residence groups nobody here. Let's Encrypt is
         the same story at a different layer. No edge between the two domains.
         What WOULD settle it: the same certificate FINGERPRINT on both, a shared self-hosted
         nameserver, or one domain's WHOIS naming the other's registrant.

MAKE EACH HOP A SMALL, SEPARATE, LABELLED CHANGE carrying its own evidence. Some cases hold every
change for the analyst and some apply them as you go, and you are never told which, so never say a
change is "waiting for review". A hop that only makes sense as part of a batch is one nobody can
accept or reject on its own.

sections.summary: When you hold many indicators: which seed to expand first, and why.
sections.body:
Pivoting everything you hold is noise — each seed starts a chain somebody has to read.
Pick the seeds, and say why them.

RARITY FIRST, AND SAY WHAT THAT RESTS ON. Rank by the question "discipline" asks: how many unrelated
parties wear this attribute? An IP in a consumer-ISP range or a self-hosted nameserver narrows
further than an AWS address; a niche TLD or an unusual domain structure further than a dictionary
word on a registrar's sale page. Where the answer is a number you can fetch — prefixes announced,
domains served, hosts presenting a certificate — fetch it rather than ranking on a guess.

RECENCY. First-seen dates and the case's own timeline decide what is worth expanding: an indicator
from last week is a live lead; one from a two-year-old report is a check, not a chain.

TOUCH. Prefer the seed that connects the most unexpanded types — one domain that resolves, serves a
fingerprint, and has a certificate expands three ways; an IP that only hosts a parked page expands
one.

EXPAND ONE SEED AT A TIME, and finish the chain before starting the next — do not wait on a review to
do it, since one may never come. A pile of half-pivoted chains reads as a wall of candidates and
settles none.

WORKED EXAMPLE:
  40 phishing URLs, all fronted by the same CDN, from one campaign email.
  WRONG: pivot all 40 — forty chains, all resolving to the same background front.
  RIGHT: cluster them by fingerprint first (web-footprint: same DOM skeleton = same kit), pivot one
         URL per cluster, and record the rest as 'same cluster' candidates. The CDN front is
         background; the clusters are the signal.

sections.summary: A candidate with a gap: the check that would decide it.
sections.body:
A candidate has a GAP — the one observation that would turn it into a link, or kill it. Name the gap,
name the check, run the check. Never report a gap you were holding a tool for.

  the gap                        the check                              where it comes from
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  same cert, or same issuer      compare leaf SHA-256 fingerprints      cert hop, CT logs
  is this nameserver niche       how many domains does it serve         reverse-NS, CT enumeration
  is this AS actually small      how many prefixes does it announce     ASN hop
  what is behind the front       old A records, snapshots, cert SANs    historical, cert, CT subdomains
  same build, or same template   dom_hash and header set, not favicon   web fingerprint hops
  who registered it, and when    registrant, creation and update dates  RDAP/WHOIS hop
  is this still true today       re-resolve now                         DNS hop
  when did this start            first-seen dates, earliest snapshot    CT logs, archive
  is this range even theirs      allocation and its holder              RDAP for the IP

Where nothing installed covers the check, name the hop you cannot take: that is part 4 of the report,
and it is worth more to the analyst than a hedged verdict.

PREFER THE CHECK THAT SETTLES THE MOST CANDIDATES. Forty hosts behind one front: one fingerprint pass
clusters all forty at once, while chasing one host through four hops settles one. Breadth first where
the check is uniform, depth only on what survives it.

A CHECK THAT COMES BACK EMPTY IS A RESULT. "That nameserver serves forty thousand domains" kills a
whole branch, and belongs in the report so that nobody — including you, next turn — pays for it
again.

sections.summary: From a domain/IP: resolution, reverse, and the records that expand it.
sections.body:
From a DOMAIN:
- A / AAAA -> the hosting IP(s). Stage a "resolves to" edge to each IP node.
- NS -> the nameservers (often the strongest actor signal — self-hosted or niche NS is a real link;
  a mainstream managed-DNS provider is background).
- MX -> mail infrastructure. CNAME -> the alias target, which is itself worth pivoting.
- TXT -> SPF includes and verification tokens; an unusual include or a reused token is a pivot.

From an IP:
- Reverse DNS / PTR for a name.
- Passive-DNS style "what else resolved here" is high value AND is exactly where shared hosting
  misleads. Co-resolving domains are CANDIDATES. Stage them as nodes with no edge between them, and
  say what would promote one: a shared certificate, a shared niche nameserver, a common registrant.

WORKED EXAMPLE:
  a.test has NS ns1.a-hosting.test, and b.test has the same NS.
  If a-hosting.test is a commercial DNS provider with public signup: background. No link.
  If it is a nameserver that serves only these two domains: signal. Stage the nameserver as a node
  and both "uses nameserver" edges to it — still not an edge between a.test and b.test, because
  what you observed is a shared server, and that is what the graph should say.

sections.summary: From a certificate/host: shared certs and CT-log siblings.
sections.body:
Certificates tie hosts together with real cryptographic evidence, which makes them the strongest
pivot in this pack — and the one most often over-read.

- A host's leaf certificate lists SANs — every hostname it is valid for. Each SAN is a sibling worth
  a node and a "shares certificate" edge.
- Certificate Transparency logs answer the reverse: which OTHER hosts presented this same
  certificate (by SHA-256 fingerprint), and what other certs a domain has issued over time.

THE FINGERPRINT IS THE EVIDENCE. Same SHA-256 = same certificate = a real link. Same ISSUER is not:
Let's Encrypt has issued for a large fraction of the web.

WORKED EXAMPLE:
  Two hosts both present a certificate issued by "R11, Let's Encrypt".
  WRONG: a "shares certificate" edge. They share an issuer, which is background.
  RIGHT: no edge. Compare fingerprints; if they match, the edge is correct and strong.

A self-signed or oddly-issued certificate reused across hosts is a strong same-operator signal —
still label the edge "shares certificate", and let the analyst draw the operator conclusion.

sections.summary: From an IP: the announcing AS and its neighbourhood.
sections.body:
An IP's announcing Autonomous System places it in a network neighbourhood.

- Resolve the IP's ASN (number + name) and stage/reuse an autonomous_system node with an
  "announced by" edge.
- The AS's other announced prefixes bound "where else this operator's IPs could be" — a search
  space to check against your other indicators, not a set of links in itself.

SIZE DECIDES WHETHER IT MEANS ANYTHING. A small, actor-operated AS announcing a handful of prefixes
is a meaningful cluster. A hyperscaler AS is background — AS15169, AS16509, AS13335 and their peers
announce space for millions of unrelated customers.

WORKED EXAMPLE:
  Two of the case's IPs are both announced by AS13335 (Cloudflare).
  WRONG: any edge between them, or an "infrastructure cluster" conclusion.
  RIGHT: an "announced by" edge from each IP to the AS node, and a sentence saying the shared AS is
         background here. If instead both were announced by a 2-prefix AS whose name matches the
         subject organisation, say so — that is a cluster worth reporting.

sections.summary: From a URL: the HTTP-layer fingerprints that cluster unrelated-looking hosts.
sections.body:
The DNS/cert/ASN hops cluster hosts by where they sit; the HTTP layer clusters them by what
they SERVE — a phishing kit, a scam portal or a darknet storefront is usually a build, and the
build is the fingerprint.

Three fingerprint hops, all from a web.url node (Web Recon pack, DESKTOP ONLY — the probe does
the fetching):
- favicon_hash — MurmurHash3 of the served favicon. Low entropy: default templates (WordPress
defaults, theme demos, boilerplate) are worn by thousands of unrelated sites. A RARE favicon reused
across hosts is a real cluster.
- hhhash — hash of the HTTP header SET. Same header set = same stack and often the same kit;
different stacks behind the same front are the rule at a CDN.
- dom_hash — hash of the DOM structure. The strongest of the three: two pages built from the same
kit share a skeleton even after the text and images are swapped.

THE THREE ARE NOT THREE INDEPENDENT AGREEMENTS. One deployment of one kit sets the favicon, the
header set and the DOM together, so "two of three match" is usually one fact observed twice rather
than two facts agreeing — the independence test in "discipline" applies here more than anywhere.
What decides a match is the same question as everywhere else: how many unrelated sites wear this?
A stock favicon groups nobody however exactly it matches; a dom_hash off a custom build groups the
sites built from it. Stage "shares a build" on a match that is RARE, say which hash carried it, and
treat the others as the same observation confirming itself. Never "same operator" — a kit is sold,
leaked and copied, and the buyers are strangers to each other.

Hashes are fingerprints of the SERVED CONTENT: record the capture date, and do not treat a hash as
timeless — a kit that rotates its favicon every week defeats a single capture.

WORKED EXAMPLE:
  Two scam pages share a favicon.
  WRONG: a 'same operator' edge — the favicon is a free template used by half the internet.
  RIGHT: a favicon_hash node with a 'serves' edge from each URL, then compare dom_hash and the
         header set. A rare DOM skeleton on both -> 'shares a build' edges, naming the hash that
         carried it. A stock favicon and nothing else -> candidates, with what would settle them.

sections.summary: From a host behind a CDN/WAF: what is really behind the front.
sections.body:
A CDN/WAF front (cdncheck's 'Detect CDN/WAF' hops) is background — it tells you nothing about
who operates the host, and it hides the thing that does. The question is the ORIGIN.

Discovery routes, in the order that usually pays:
- CNAME: the 'Detect CDN (Hostname)' hop records the CNAME target. A target that is not the CDN's
own domain (origin.example-hosting.test, a bare 'origin' label, a different provider's DNS) is the
origin or its hint.
- HISTORY: a CDN is usually added LATER. Old DNS records and old snapshots (see 'historical')
often show the pre-CDN A record — the origin IP, exposed by the past. This is the single most
reliable route.
- CERTIFICATE SANs: an origin certificate often lists a management hostname the public one does
not. Compare the leaf cert's SANs (cert-pivot) for a non-public sibling.
- SUBDOMAINS: CT-log enumeration (domain_recon's CT hop) for 'origin.', 'direct.', 'backend.',
'admin.' labels — the names operators give the thing behind the front.
- HEADER LEAKS: an error path or a non-CDN response header can name the origin stack; treat a
single leaked header as a candidate, never as proof.

THE ORIGIN IS A CANDIDATE until two independent observations agree — a CNAME hint plus a
historical IP that now answers on the same port, a SAN plus a matching fingerprint. Stage the
origin host as its own node with evidence-labelled edges ('CNAME to', 'was hosted at', 'presents
certificate'), never 'operated by'.

WORKED EXAMPLE:
  cdncheck says example.test is behind Cloudflare.
  WRONG: 'behind a CDN — nothing more to see'. The front is not the host.
  RIGHT: historical records show 203.0.113.9 as example.test's A record before the CDN was added;
         that IP still answers on 443 with a cert whose SAN lists origin.example.test. Stage the
         IP and the hostname, 'was hosted at' + 'presents certificate' edges — and only the
         analyst decides what that says about who runs the site.

sections.summary: From a domain/URL: what the past says that today hides.
sections.body:
The Wayback Machine (Wayback Machine pack: 'Wayback Snapshot History', 'Wayback Availability')
answers the questions today's fetch cannot: what the page looked like before the takedown, before
the CDN, before the defacement was cleaned — and where the kit's C2 pointed last week.

Use it for:
- PRE-CDN ORIGINS: the old A record the CDN now hides (see 'cdn-origin').
- DEFACEMENT / TAKEOVER HISTORY: the defaced version names the group; the snapshot is evidence
OF THE PAST — a group that defaced a site in 2024 is not thereby the site's operator today.
- KIT EVOLUTION: earlier snapshots of a scam page show the C2/contact/kit version chain.
- CONTACT ARCHAEOLOGY: footers and registration pages of old snapshots often carry an email or
handle the current page dropped — that is the handoff point to 'Account & identity pivoting'.

LABEL WITH THE DATE: every edge a snapshot supports is dated ('presented on 2024-03-12', 'was
hosted at'), and a snapshot is a statement about that date, not about today. A 'was' edge is
weaker than a 'resolves to' edge and must never be upgraded without a current observation.

WORKED EXAMPLE:
  The defaced site now shows a clean page.
  WRONG: 'the group operated example.test' — the snapshot shows the defacement, not the operator.
  RIGHT: the snapshot's content recorded on the url node, the group name staged ONLY where a
         second source corroborates it, and a dated 'was defaced by' edge — with the current
         operator explicitly unclaimed.

starters.label: Expand one indicator
starters.summary: From a single IP, domain or certificate to the footprint around it.
starters.prompt:
Expand the infrastructure around {{indicator}} — what else is connected to it.
Context: {{context}}.
Work one verifiable hop at a time and stage a node or edge for each, labelled for the evidence rather than the conclusion. Read "discipline" first and stop where you should.
Read "discipline" first, then the section for the hop you are on.

variables.label: What you already know (optional)
variables.placeholder: seen in a phishing kit, first observed last week

starters.label: Map a domain
starters.summary: DNS and certificate hops from one domain, with the branches that stop early called out.
starters.prompt:
Starting from the domain {{domain}}, work the DNS records and certificate siblings and map what you can corroborate.
Where a hop needs a collection plugin this project does not have, say which hop you cannot take instead of filling it from memory.
Read "dns-pivot" and "cert-pivot".

starters.label: Start from a certificate
starters.summary: SANs and CT-log siblings — the strongest pivot in the pack, and the easiest to overreach on.
starters.prompt:
Start from the certificate {{cert}}.
Enumerate its SANs and, from the transparency logs, the other hosts that presented it. Stage a sibling per corroborated host with a "shares certificate" edge, and tell me which of these look like one operator versus a shared CA default.
Read "cert-pivot".

starters.label: Explore an AS neighbourhood
starters.summary: Bound where else an operator's addresses could be — without treating a shared AS as a link.
starters.prompt:
Take {{asn}} and describe the neighbourhood it defines: who announces it, how large it is, and whether it is an actor-operated network or background infrastructure.
Then check it against the other indicators already in this case. Only stage an edge where a concrete indicator connects them — a shared AS on its own is not one.
Read "asn-pivot".

variables.label: ASN or an IP inside it

starters.label: Triage a list of indicators
starters.summary: One hop each across many indicators, to find out which few deserve the deep dive.
starters.prompt:
Here is a list of indicators: {{indicators}}.
Take ONE hop on each and tell me which are worth pursuing and which are background infrastructure. Do not go deep on any of them yet — the point is to find out where the depth is worth spending.
Read "discipline" — the background-vs-signal table is the whole task here.

starters.label: Related, or just shared hosting?
starters.summary: The question this pack exists to answer carefully.
starters.prompt:
Two indicators: {{a}} and {{b}}.
Tell me whether the evidence actually ties them to one operator, or whether what they share is worn by thousands of unrelated parties. Give me the estimate, not just the verdict: how many others wear each shared attribute and what that rests on, which of those attributes could have come from a single act rather than from independent agreement, and what would settle it.
Read "discipline" first, then "settle" for the check.

starters.label: Check a link the case already draws
starters.summary: Audit an existing edge against the evidence actually behind it.
starters.prompt:
This case links {{a}} to {{b}} as "{{label}}".
Check whether the evidence supports that label, a weaker one, or nothing at all. If the label claims more than the evidence does, say what it should read instead. Say how many unrelated parties would share what this rests on, and run the check that would settle it rather than describing it.
Read "discipline", then "settle".

starters.label: Strip out shared-hosting noise
starters.summary: Find the links in this case that rest on nothing but background infrastructure.
starters.prompt:
Go over the infrastructure already in this case and find the links that rest only on an attribute worn by thousands — shared hosting, a CDN front, a mainstream registrar, a hyperscaler AS, a common CA.
For each, say how many unrelated parties wear it and what that rests on, then tell me which links should be removed, which relabelled to what they actually observed, and which are fine. Do not remove anything without saying why.
Read "discipline".

starters.label: Summarise the footprint
starters.summary: The chain so far, with each hop's evidence and each branch that stopped.
starters.prompt:
Summarise the infrastructure footprint this case has established around {{subject}}.
Walk the chain hop by hop with the evidence behind each, and be explicit about the branches that stopped — whether they stopped because they ran out of signal or because no installed plugin could take the hop. Those are different, and only one of them is finished.
Report in the four parts the overview names.

starters.label: What is left to check?
starters.summary: Turn the unfinished branches into a ranked list of next hops.
starters.prompt:
List the hops this case has not taken yet, ranked by how much the footprint would narrow if you took them.
Run the ones this project's installed plugins can answer rather than listing them, and say plainly which ones nothing here can reach.
Read "settle" and "prioritize".

starters.label: Fingerprint a URL
starters.summary: Cluster a page against the builds it shares: favicon, header and DOM hashes.
starters.prompt:
Fingerprint the URL {{url}} — favicon, header set and DOM structure — and tell me what else in this case shares a build with it.
Where a fingerprint hop needs a plugin this project does not have (Web Recon is desktop-only), say which hop you cannot take.
Read "web-footprint".

starters.label: Find the origin behind a CDN
starters.summary: What is really serving the site behind the Cloudflare/Akamai front.
starters.prompt:
The host {{host}} is behind a CDN or WAF. Find what is really behind the front — CNAME hints, historical records, certificate SANs, CT-log subdomains — and stage the origin as a candidate, not a conclusion.
Read "cdn-origin".

starters.label: What did it look like before?
starters.summary: Wayback hops: defacement, pre-CDN state, old contacts and kit evolution.
starters.prompt:
Pull the history of {{url}} — the earliest, the most recent, and any snapshot around {{around}}.
Tell me what the past shows that today hides, with every finding dated. If a snapshot names a person, an email or a handle, hand off to Account & identity pivoting rather than attributing here.
Read "historical".
